https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/02/dr-c.text: The Ebola outbreak, officially detected in mid-May, has hit unstable regions in the vast central African country where armed clashes and violence, alongside a critical lack of resources, have hindered the health response to the deadly virus in recent days.According to the latest official data, there have been 4,018 fatalities from 8,300 cases, with 2,162 people recovering, giving a fatality rate to date of 48.4 percent.Also recorded have been four deaths among six cases in North Kivu province in the northeast in areas controlled by the anti-government group M23, the Kigali-backed group stated Friday.After starting in Ituri, also in the northeast, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.The response has been hindered by conflict but also mistrust of authority which runs deep among inhabitants of several provinces.Violent clashes disturbing health aidRecent days have seen violent clashes between local militias that have hampered the response in Ituri, with more than 5,000 people displaced, the UN said on Thursday.A transit centre for Ebola patients burned down Tuesday in the same province after soldiers entered a site for displaced people who promptly fled, according to the UN.A contractor responsible for detecting cases was also killed in an attack on a health facility in North Kivu province, Congolese authorities said Wednesday.French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot was due in Ituri capital Bunia on Friday to show Paris' support for local authorities and humanitarian workers.There is no indication France is offering fresh humanitarian aid, but the country did allocate €13.4M to the fight against Ebola between January and July.The United States has meanwhile announced it is releasing a further €237M to combat the spread of the disease.Healthcare workers are notably at risk of contracting the virus in poor and remote regions where healthcare infrastructure is poor.Several vaccines and treatments are currently being studied to combat the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which is behind the current outbreak.The first doses of the Ervebo vaccine — which has been proven effective against the Zaire strain, the most common variant, in the past — have been administered in recent weeks to volunteers among frontline staff as part of a clinical trial.

(Photo by Sergei SUPINSKY / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip European leaders and top diplomats rallied behind Ukraine after Russia’s latest attacks on Kyiv struck the National Academy of Sciences, a medical facility and other civilian sites, with officials accusing Moscow of targeting civilians, science and critical infrastructure. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attack demonstrated that Ukraine’s scientific community had itself become a target. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Today, science became a target for Russia,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “My heart goes out to the heroes searching for people trapped inside Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. As well as to the families and loved ones of the victims of horrific attacks across the country.” “We stand with them. And with all Ukrainians,” she added. “Europe is working harder than ever to strengthen Ukraine’s defence.” Advertisement The international condemnation followed a day of Russian strikes across Kyiv on Sept. 28 that killed two people and injured 26, according to Kyiv authorities. The Academy building was among several civilian sites hit during the attacks. A pharmaceutical company and medical facility were also struck, while damage was reported across multiple districts of the capital. France: Russia Is ‘Targeting Civilians and Knowledge’ France’s Embassy in Ukraine placed the attack on the Academy alongside previous Russian strikes on educational institutions in Kyiv. Other Topics of Interest Zelensky Warns Russia Is Training North Korea for War, Feeding Iran Satellite Intelligence Kyiv says Russia is preparing more North Korean troops while sharing satellite intelligence with Iran on US and Gulf military sites. “Schools, universities of Kyiv, and now the Academy of Sciences, struck in broad daylight, set ablaze, just steps from the Opera,” the embassy wrote on X . “By targeting civilians and knowledge, Russia is pursuing its escalation of terror. This cruelty will not go unpunished. France stands alongside Ukraine.” Austria: Attacks Are ‘Absolutely Appalling’ Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker highlighted both the strike on the Academy and the attack on a medical facility in central Kyiv. “Russia’s attacks on Ukraine are absolutely appalling and must stop!” Stocker wrote on X . Advertisement “A clinic and the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv’s city center have been hit, and there has been near-constant bombardment for days.” “Deliberately targeting civilians and carrying out acts of terror against the civilian population is reprehensible and a violation of international law,” he added. Norway: ‘Civilian Institutions Must Not Be Targets’ Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide also singled out the National Academy strike. “I am appalled by Russia’s latest attacks across Ukraine, including on the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv,” Eide wrote on X . “Scientists and staff should be able to work safely. Civilian institutions must not be targets of attacks. Norway stands firmly with Ukraine.” Spain: Attacks Violate International Humanitarian Law Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares accused Russia of continuing to strike civilian targets. Spain’s Foreign Ministry identifies Albares as the country’s current minister for foreign affairs, European Union and cooperation. “I firmly condemn the continued attacks by Russia against civilian targets in Ukraine, in clear violation of international humanitarian law,” Albares wrote on X. Lithuania Warns of ‘Reckless Escalation’ Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys went beyond the Kyiv strikes, warning about attacks near Ukraine’s border with Poland and routes used for international assistance. Advertisement “Strongly condemn Russia’s latest attacks against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, hitting the National Academy of Sciences, hospitals, and civilian infrastructure,” Budrys wrote on X . He described Russian attacks near the Polish-Ukrainian border and along critical international assistance routes as “a reckless act of escalation.” “Efforts to intimidate Ukraine and obstruct support are doomed to fail,” he said. “They will not weaken our resolve – we will continue supporting Ukraine and strengthening the pressure on Russia.” Academy Strike Draws Particular Outrage The National Academy of Sciences strike carried additional symbolic weight because the institution sits at the center of Ukraine’s scientific and academic establishment. The attack caused a fire and prompted a rescue operation inside the building. Early reports from Kyiv authorities said one person had been killed and several others injured at the Academy site. President Volodymyr Zelensky said emergency crews were searching for people who might still be trapped inside, stressing that the Academy was only one of several civilian sites struck across Ukraine that day. Advertisement “Every Russian act of terror results in casualties that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total – pressure on everything that finances and produces Russia’s weapons of terror, and on everyone who uses them,” Zelensky said. “The world must understand that terrorists will keep going if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine.” “And such brutal strikes must not be ignored. There must be a response – with global resolve and strength.” “We are counting on the strength of Europe, America, and our other partners who can help protect lives.” To suggest a correction or clarification, write to us here You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter Contact Us Please leave your suggestions or corrections here Cancel Send Kyiv Post Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-bla.text: BRUSSELS — NATO allies will hold a crisis meeting to discuss how to respond to a series of drone strikes on cargo shipping in the Black Sea, Romania’s President Nicușor Dan said. Two chemical tankers were hit by air drones in the past 24 hours in or near Romania’s territorial waters, but it is “too early” to say for sure whether Russia was behind the attacks, Dan added. Dan was speaking on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels, where he spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte about the latest incidents. Advertisement Advertisement “The secretary general expressed the solidarity of the alliance and there will be a NAC [North Atlantic Council] meeting at which the whole situation with the Black Sea will be discussed,” Dan told POLITICO. “Of course the conclusion is that all the hybrid attacks are trying to decrease our support for Ukraine. We will continue to support,” he said. Dan said invoking NATO’s collective defense clause, Article 5, was “not now” being discussed as an option for responding to the attacks. Nor has Romania asked for Article 4 — the emergency clause that sets consultations in motion over military matters when a member’s security has been threatened — to be triggered, he said. Rescuers are searching for seven missing crew members after two chemical tankers were hit by aerial drones in or near Romanian territorial waters . Over the past 10 days, drones have hit at least five more cargo ships close to Romania and Bulgaria — both NATO members — killing at least 23 sailors. Investigation teams from Romania's army and intelligence services are trying to establish what led to the most recent drones strikes on the ships, Dan said. Romania asked NATO for equipment including specialized radars and requested the delivery to be accelerated after a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building near the border with Ukraine in May. Dan suggested Romania was likely to seek further assistance with equipment from allies this time. “On the operational level, we are in the same situation where we have been … on the Danube border with Ukraine,” Dan said. “What we did at that moment, we came here to NATO and some of our allies — United States, France, Spain, Italy, Slovakia, Portugal — gave us some equipment. And now we are in the same situation, but on the other border, with the Black Sea.” After the meeting with Dan and Radev, NATO’s Rutte said the alliance had already increased “counter-drone capabilities” along its eastern flank. “NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he posted on X. This story has been updated. Victor Jack contributed to the report. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has admitted ‘it was not correct’ to say a $6m grant to Marrickville golf club in his electorate was for sewerage works. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP View image in fullscreen The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has admitted ‘it was not correct’ to say a $6m grant to Marrickville golf club in his electorate was for sewerage works. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP Anthony Albanese Albanese concedes $6m golf club grant in his electorate was not to contain ‘raw sewage’ Grant part of $560m invitation-only scheme transparency advocates say largely funded projects in Labor-held seats Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Basford Canales and Kat Wong Tue 27 Oct 2026 04.52 EDT First published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 02.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Anthony Albanese has admitted he got it wrong after telling parliament a $6m grant to a golf club in his electorate was to stop “raw sewage” going into the nearby river. The grant given to Marrickville golf club in Sydney’s inner-west is under scrutiny as part of a larger $560m invitation-only grants scheme, which transparency advocates say largely funded projects promised at the 2025 election in Labor-held seats. Infrastructure department officials told a Senate estimates hearing on Monday afternoon the $6m grant given to the club in Albanese’s electorate did not fund works to prevent raw sewage from flowing into the nearby river, contrary to the prime minister’s claims. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “I can confirm that sewerage is not a component of this grant,” the department’s assistant secretary, Jacinta McDonald, said. The assistant regional development minister, Anthony Chisholm, defended the prime minister’s response, saying the scope had changed since the local council’s original proposal. “I think that was part of the original plan. But as often happens, as the scope of these sorts of announcements happen, the scope can change, and the New South Wales government, is my understanding, stepped in in support of the sewerage work,” Chisholm said. First reported by the ABC , Albanese, who holds honorary social membership at the club, has swatted away any criticism that he influenced, or benefitted from, the decision, which was signed off by another minister. Constitutional expert labels Albanese government’s golf club grant ‘grey corruption’ Read more In question time in early September, the prime minister told the house the money would go toward “an environmental project stopping raw sewage going into the Cooks River during flooding”. “[The golf club] has existed for a long time, almost a 100 years, and they have a septic tank because it is on the floodplain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River – that is what the funding is for,” Albanese said in another response to questions about his involvement in the decision-making process. The prime minister was grilled repeatedly by the opposition about the grant in question time on Tuesday afternoon and the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, accused the prime minister of misleading the parliament, and urged him to correct the record. In response, Albanese conceded “it was not correct” to say the funding was for sewerage works but said it was a matter for the infrastructure department, and noted the council was finalising the design of the project – including improvements to the clubhouse, stormwater harvesting, a new toilet and landscaping. The NSW government committed in September 2025 to address sewerage infrastructure at the club, he said. “I’m advised that the club, of course, has a long history. And indeed, in the media release announcing the project, it spoke about the venue’s last major remodel being in 1947. So this is a local club, owned by the council,” Albanese said. “The [federal] funding was going to be for sewerage. The New South Wales government have stepped in, which is appropriate given that New South Wales run water and sewerage.” Explore more on these topics Anthony Albanese Australian politics news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Are you waiting for me to be attacked?’ Fatima Payman slams PM over office security Labor condemns One Nation cartoons depicting Penny Wong being murdered as Hanson says videos ‘not going anywhere’ The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns Angus Taylor criticised for ‘tone deaf’ response to alleged attack on Helen Haines Helen Haines’s first words after alleged attack revealed as MPs honour her ‘empathy and grace’ Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters
